I just feel too tense and guilty to even enjoy my usual stress-relievers like hiking or yoga anymore.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any recurring, distressing memories or thoughts about your husband's diagnosis that you can't seem to get out of your mind?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I have distressing memories or flashbacks of the actual moment he was diagnosed. It's more that I constantly struggle with anxious, intrusive thoughts about the future, often lying awake at night running through worst-case scenarios about how his condition will progress.\n\nDoctor: Are these intrusive thoughts about the future and worst-case scenarios related to your husband's diagnosis specifically, or are they more general worries about other aspects of your life as well?\n\nPatient: They are almost entirely tied to my husband's diagnosis and what the future holds for his health and my role as his caregiver. I'm not really worrying about other unrelated things, though the stress from this is definitely spilling over and making me highly reactive and irritable at my job.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me when exactly these feelings of being overwhelmed and intrusive thoughts about your husband's diagnosis started - was it immediately after his diagnosis, or did they develop over time as his condition progressed?\n\nPatient: They didn't start the exact day of his diagnosis, but rather developed within a few weeks after it. These feelings have really been building up over the last two months, especially during that first wave of specialist appointments and treatment planning.\n\nDoctor: Did these feelings of being overwhelmed and intrusive thoughts about your husband's diagnosis start within hours or days of a specific stressful event related to his diagnosis, or did they develop more gradually over a period of weeks?\n\nPatient: They definitely developed more gradually over a few weeks rather than starting right away. Within a few weeks of his diagnosis, I noticed myself becoming unusually irritable, tearful after appointments, and too keyed up to sleep. These feelings have really been building over the last two months as the caregiving tasks and specialist visits piled up.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned these feelings developed over a few weeks after your husband's diagnosis. Have these symptoms persisted at the same level of intensity over the last two months, or have you noticed any fluctuations?\n\nPatient: They have been quite consistent and have actually been building up rather than fluctuating or getting better. Ever since that first wave of specialist visits, these feelings have felt constant and overwhelming as I try to manage everything.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced significant fatigue or a notable decrease in your energy levels alongside these feelings of being overwhelmed and anxious about your husband's diagnosis?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed distinct physical fatigue or low energy. Instead, I just feel constantly keyed up, anxious, and unable to sleep because my mind is always racing.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself avoiding certain activities, places, or conversations because they remind you of your husband's diagnosis or make you feel even more overwhelmed and anxious?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've been avoiding almost all of my usual social and recreational activities lately. I’ve completely stopped going on weekend hikes with my hiking group, skipped my yoga classes, and put aside knitting and going to the theater. I just feel too wound up, anxious, and guilty to enjoy them, like I shouldn't be out having fun when there is so much caregiving and work to manage.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if avoiding these activities is primarily because they remind you of your husband's diagnosis, or is it more because you feel guilty enjoying yourself while he's going through this, or perhaps because you're just too anxious and overwhelmed to participate in them?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both guilt and anxiety. I feel guilty taking time for myself to enjoy things while my husband is going through this diagnosis. On top of that, I just feel far too wound up and anxious to actually relax or get any enjoyment out of those activities anyway.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific situations, conversations, or reminders related to your husband's diagnosis that you're actively trying to avoid, and if so, what are they?\n\nPatient: I don't feel like I'm actively avoiding reminders or conversations about his diagnosis; if anything, I feel completely consumed by managing his appointments and treatment. I'm really not sure if there is anything specific related to his illness that I'm trying to avoid.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned avoiding social and recreational activities due to feeling guilty and anxious, but are there any specific aspects of your husband's diagnosis or treatment that you find yourself trying to avoid thinking about or confronting?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way. Whenever I think about going on hikes or doing yoga, I feel a deep sense of guilt for taking time for myself while my husband is dealing with this. I am just too keyed up and tense to actually relax or enjoy those activities anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your avoidance of activities is primarily to reduce your distress related to your husband's diagnosis, or is it more about feeling guilty for potentially enjoying yourself during this time?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both. I feel far too wound up, anxious, and overwhelmed to actually relax and enjoy any of my hobbies right now. At the same time, I carry a deep sense of guilt about taking time for myself to enjoy things while my husband is dealing with his new diagnosis.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if your husband's health condition were to stabilize or improve, you would be able to return to and enjoy your previously avoided activities, or do you think your avoidance of them has become a more ingrained pattern of behavior for you?\n\nPatient: I believe that once we get through this initial wave of appointments and settle into a stable routine with his treatment, I'll be able to return to my normal schedule. I keep telling myself that I'll be able to resume my hobbies like hiking and yoga and finally feel more like myself again. It doesn't feel like a permanent pattern, just a reaction to how overwhelmed I am right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the avoidance of your usual activities is a way to escape from the emotional pain related to your husband's diagnosis, or is it more about not knowing how to cope with the stress and anxiety it brings?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both. I've also found myself snapping at coworkers over small errors and crying in my car after his medical appointments. I just feel too tense and guilty to even enjoy my usual stress-relievers like hiking or yoga anymore.\n\nDoctor: Have you been experiencing any recurring, distressing memories or thoughts about your husband's diagnosis that you can't seem to get out of your mind?\n\nPatient: I wouldn't say I have distressing memories or flashbacks of the actual moment he was diagnosed. It's more that I constantly struggle with anxious, intrusive thoughts about the future, often lying awake at night running through worst-case scenarios about how his condition will progress.\n\nDoctor: Are these intrusive thoughts about the future and worst-case scenarios related to your husband's diagnosis specifically, or are they more general worries about other aspects of your life as well?\n\nPatient: They are almost entirely tied to my husband's diagnosis and what the future holds for his health and my role as his caregiver. I'm not really worrying about other unrelated things, though the stress from this is definitely spilling over and making me highly reactive and irritable at my job.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me when exactly these feelings of being overwhelmed and intrusive thoughts about your husband's diagnosis started - was it immediately after his diagnosis, or did they develop over time as his condition progressed?\n\nPatient: They didn't start the exact day of his diagnosis, but rather developed within a few weeks after it. These feelings have really been building up over the last two months, especially during that first wave of specialist appointments and treatment planning.\n\nDoctor: Did these feelings of being overwhelmed and intrusive thoughts about your husband's diagnosis start within hours or days of a specific stressful event related to his diagnosis, or did they develop more gradually over a period of weeks?\n\nPatient: They definitely developed more gradually over a few weeks rather than starting right away. Within a few weeks of his diagnosis, I noticed myself becoming unusually irritable, tearful after appointments, and too keyed up to sleep. These feelings have really been building over the last two months as the caregiving tasks and specialist visits piled up.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned these feelings developed over a few weeks after your husband's diagnosis. Have these symptoms persisted at the same level of intensity over the last two months, or have you noticed any fluctuations?\n\nPatient: They have been quite consistent and have actually been building up rather than fluctuating or getting better. Ever since that first wave of specialist visits, these feelings have felt constant and overwhelming as I try to manage everything.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced significant fatigue or a notable decrease in your energy levels alongside these feelings of being overwhelmed and anxious about your husband's diagnosis?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed distinct physical fatigue or low energy. Instead, I just feel constantly keyed up, anxious, and unable to sleep because my mind is always racing.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself avoiding certain activities, places, or conversations because they remind you of your husband's diagnosis or make you feel even more overwhelmed and anxious?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've been avoiding almost all of my usual social and recreational activities lately. I’ve completely stopped going on weekend hikes with my hiking group, skipped my yoga classes, and put aside knitting and going to the theater. I just feel too wound up, anxious, and guilty to enjoy them, like I shouldn't be out having fun when there is so much caregiving and work to manage.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if avoiding these activities is primarily because they remind you of your husband's diagnosis, or is it more because you feel guilty enjoying yourself while he's going through this, or perhaps because you're just too anxious and overwhelmed to participate in them?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both guilt and anxiety. I feel guilty taking time for myself to enjoy things while my husband is going through this diagnosis. On top of that, I just feel far too wound up and anxious to actually relax or get any enjoyment out of those activities anyway.\n\nDoctor: Are there any specific situations, conversations, or reminders related to your husband's diagnosis that you're actively trying to avoid, and if so, what are they?\n\nPatient: I don't feel like I'm actively avoiding reminders or conversations about his diagnosis; if anything, I feel completely consumed by managing his appointments and treatment. I'm really not sure if there is anything specific related to his illness that I'm trying to avoid.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned avoiding social and recreational activities due to feeling guilty and anxious, but are there any specific aspects of your husband's diagnosis or treatment that you find yourself trying to avoid thinking about or confronting?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way. Instead of avoiding his diagnosis or treatment, I feel like I'm constantly overthinking and worrying about every single aspect of it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your avoidance of social and recreational activities is an attempt to cope with your anxiety and guilt, or is it more because you're trying to prevent yourself from feeling even more overwhelmed by reminders of your husband's diagnosis?\n\nPatient: It isn't about avoiding reminders of his diagnosis, but rather that I feel too anxious and guilty to even participate. Whenever I think about going on hikes or doing yoga, I feel a deep sense of guilt for taking time for myself while my husband is dealing with this. I am just too keyed up and tense to actually relax or enjoy those activities anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your avoidance of activities is primarily to reduce your distress related to your husband's diagnosis, or is it more about feeling guilty for potentially enjoying yourself during this time?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both. I feel far too wound up, anxious, and overwhelmed to actually relax and enjoy any of my hobbies right now. At the same time, I carry a deep sense of guilt about taking time for myself to enjoy things while my husband is dealing with his new diagnosis.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if your husband's health condition were to stabilize or improve, you would be able to return to and enjoy your previously avoided activities, or do you think your avoidance of them has become a more ingrained pattern of behavior for you?\n\nPatient: I believe that once we get through this initial wave of appointments and settle into a stable routine with his treatment, I'll be able to return to my normal schedule. I keep telling myself that I'll be able to resume my hobbies like hiking and yoga and finally feel more like myself again. It doesn't feel like a permanent pattern, just a reaction to how overwhelmed I am right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the avoidance of your usual activities is a way to escape from the emotional pain related to your husband's diagnosis, or is it more about not knowing how to cope with the stress and anxiety it brings?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both. I feel so wound up and overwhelmed by the caregiving responsibilities that I can't focus on or enjoy things like hiking or yoga. On top of that, I feel a deep sense of guilt for taking time for myself while my husband is dealing with his diagnosis.\n\nDoctor: Are your symptoms, such as feeling overwhelmed and having intrusive thoughts, exclusively related to your husband's diagnosis and caregiving responsibilities, or have you experienced similar reactions to other stressful life events in the past?\n\nPatient: Yes, these reactions are completely tied to my husband's diagnosis and the sudden caregiving responsibilities. This feels entirely new to me, almost like a switch flipped when he got diagnosed, and I've never experienced this level of unmanageable stress in the past. I've always been able to handle life's challenges much better than this.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your symptoms are almost entirely tied to your husband's diagnosis, but can you think of any other highly stressful events in your past where you might have experienced similar feelings of being overwhelmed, or is this truly the first time you've felt this way?\n\nPatient: This is truly the first time I have ever felt this level of overwhelm. I cannot recall any past events in my life where I reacted this way or felt so completely unable to manage my stress.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if there was a specific moment or event related to your husband's diagnosis that triggered these feelings, or if they gradually developed over time as you adjusted to the new situation?\n\nPatient: While the initial diagnosis three months ago was certainly a shock, the overwhelming feelings actually built up gradually over the next few weeks. As I began coordinating his specialist appointments, researching treatments, and juggling caregiving with my demanding job over the last two months, the stress and anxiety really started to compound and interfere with my daily life.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that your symptoms developed gradually over a few weeks after your husband's diagnosis, but can you tell me if there was a specific point or event within those weeks that you felt marked the beginning of your current state, or was it a completely gradual process without a clear starting point?\n\nPatient: While the diagnosis itself was an immediate shock that felt like a switch flipped, the actual symptoms and feeling overwhelmed built up gradually over the next few weeks. It really started to snowball as I began coordinating his first wave of specialist visits, researching treatments, and trying to manage my demanding work schedule all at once.\n\nDoctor: Did your symptoms start within days of a specific stressful event related to your husband's diagnosis, or did they take longer to develop, considering you've mentioned a gradual build-up over a few weeks?\n\nPatient: They didn't start within just a few days; they took a few weeks to really develop. As the reality of the diagnosis set in and we began the first wave of specialist visits and treatment planning, the stress and symptoms gradually escalated. It has really been building and bothering me over the last two months as I've tried to juggle everything.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed feeling detached from others or emotionally numb since your husband's diagnosis, or is it more that you're feeling overwhelmed by your emotions?\n\nPatient: I definitely don't feel numb or detached at all. It's quite the opposite—I feel completely overwhelmed by my emotions and feel like I'm overreacting to everything. I find myself snapping at my coworkers, crying in my car, and feeling far too wound up and guilty to enjoy my usual activities.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned feeling overwhelmed by your emotions, but can you tell me if there are any moments where you feel like you're just going through the motions or feeling disconnected from the people and activities around you?"

Instead of avoiding his diagnosis or treatment, I feel like I'm constantly overthinking and worrying about every single aspect of it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your avoidance of social and recreational activities is an attempt to cope with your anxiety and guilt, or is it more because you're trying to prevent yourself from feeling even more overwhelmed by reminders of your husband's diagnosis?\n\nPatient: It isn't about avoiding reminders of his diagnosis, but rather that I feel too anxious and guilty to even participate. Whenever I think about going on hikes or doing yoga, I feel a deep sense of guilt for taking time for myself while my husband is dealing with this. I am just too keyed up and tense to actually relax or enjoy those activities anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that your avoidance of activities is primarily to reduce your distress related to your husband's diagnosis, or is it more about feeling guilty for potentially enjoying yourself during this time?\n\nPatient: It is really a combination of both. It doesn't feel like a permanent pattern, just a reaction to how overwhelmed I am right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the avoidance of your usual activities is a way to escape from the emotional pain related to your husband's diagnosis, or is it more about not knowing how to cope with the stress and anxiety it brings?\n\nPatient: It’s really a mix of both. Instead, I just feel constantly keyed up, anxious, and unable to sleep because my mind is always racing.\n\nDoctor: Have you found yourself avoiding certain activities, places, or conversations because they remind you of your husband's diagnosis or make you feel even more overwhelmed and anxious?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've been avoiding almost all of my usual social and recreational activities lately. I feel guilty taking time for myself to enjoy things while my husband is going through this diagnosis. I'm really not sure if there is anything specific related to his illness that I'm trying to avoid.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned avoiding social and recreational activities due to feeling guilty and anxious, but are there any specific aspects of your husband's diagnosis or treatment that you find yourself trying to avoid thinking about or confronting?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure, and I haven't thought about it that way.
